item.title: Quantum synchronization in atom-cavity coupled systems
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Atom-mediated coupling induces limit cycles in undriven cavity modes and out-of-phase quantum synchronization when driven weakly, with Wehrl mutual information showing strict anti-correlation with field synchronization.

Grade 0.447 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Katha Haldar, Anushree Dey, Saikat Ghosh, Bimalendu Deb

Figure

Husimi-Q distribution Qfield(θ,ϕ), synchronization measure Sfield(ϕ), and single-mode Wigner distributions Wi(xi,pi) for weak cavity drives Ω1=Ω2=0.005Γd, showing phase localization and out-of-phase synchronization across the two cavity modes.

Asks

Can atom-mediated coupling between two driven cavity modes induce a two-mode quantum limit cycle and generate phase-locked field dynamics?

But

Requires strong-coupling cavity QED regime with cavity decay rates κ1,κ2≪g1,g2,Ωi, and large excited-state detuning |Δd|≫gi,Ω,Γd.

Tools

effective operator adiabatic elimination · SU(2) coherent states over Fock subspaces · generalized two-mode Husimi-Q function · Wehrl mutual information · quantum trajectory method

Abstract

We consider a cavity quantum electrodynamics (CQED) setup where an ensemble of spin-1 atoms driven by a classical field interacts with two driven cavity field modes. We show that the two sub-systems - the atoms and the two-mode cavity field, exhibit limit-cycle or quantum synchronization depending on the cavity drive strengths and other system parameters. In order to visualize the limit cycle and synchronization in the field, we introduce generalized two-mode field Husimi-Q function using SU(2) coherent states. For atomic spin states, we make use of spin-1 Husimi-Q function to visualize the same. We further corroborate the occurrence of field synchronization and limit cycle by analyzing U(1) symmetry breaking, Wigner quasi-probability distribution, coherence properties of reduced field density matrix. Our results reveal intriguing interplay between the limit-cycle and quantum synchronization behavior, highlighting emergent quantum phenomena in driven dissipative interacting quantum systems. Additionally, we calculate Wehrl mutual information between the two modes and find that the field synchronization and Wehrl mutual information are mutually exclusive. Our study would be important to extract quantum advantages in quantum metrology using coupled atom-cavity systems.

item.title: Loss-tolerant distributed lattice surgery using fusion networks
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Hybrid fusion-network protocols for distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery reach 50% interface-erasure threshold without local noise. Hybrid protocols using linear cluster states increase merge-observable interface distance from d+1 to 2d+1 and restore perpendicular-observable interface distance from ⌊(d+1)/2⌋ to d.

Grade 0.434 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Felix Burt, Richard Meister, Sheng-Ku Lin, Kuan-Cheng Chen, Michael Hanks, Roberto Bondesan, M. S. Kim, Kin K. Leung

Asks

How to design loss-tolerant distributed lattice surgery protocols across probabilistic photonic interfaces between networked quantum processing units.

Before

Straight Bell-pair interface geometry had merge-observable interface distance d+1 and perpendicular-observable interface distance ⌊(d+1)/2⌋.

But

Local noise masked interface-distance advantage at circuit and resource-state error rates of 10−3; improvements require local noise rates of 10−4 or below. Evaluated via numerical thresholds and simulations.

Tools

ZX calculus transformations · fusion-based quantum computing (FBQC) · distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery · fusion boosting

Abstract

Networking matter-based quantum processing units (QPUs) offers a promising route to scaling fault-tolerant quantum computers. This requires distributed logical operations to be performed across photonic links, where noise is characteristically different from and stronger than in local QPUs owing to photon loss and probabilistic linear-optical operations. Measurement- and fusion-based quantum computing are designed to be robust against loss and probabilistic photonic operations, suggesting they could complement circuit-based error correction at the interface between networked QPUs. We use ZX calculus transformations to construct hybrid syndrome extraction protocols and apply them to distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery, demonstrating that several protocols attain a 50% interface-erasure threshold when local noise is absent, including circuit-based lattice surgery using fused Bell pairs and hybrid protocols using linear cluster states. Relative to a straight Bell-pair interface geometry, the hybrid protocols increase the merge-observable interface distance from d+1 to 2d+1 and restore the perpendicular-observable interface distance from lfloor(d+1)/2rfloor to d. We calculate how the threshold decreases when using truncated resource states and map correctable regions under resource-state errors, local circuit noise, and fusion erasure. We then convert these erasure thresholds into photon-loss thresholds and probe subthreshold performance using fusion boosting. At circuit and resource-state error rates of 10⁻³, local errors largely mask the interface-distance advantage. As local noise is reduced to 10⁻⁴ and below, the linear-chain protocols improve more rapidly with decreasing erasure, suggesting that interface distance enhancements are effective in low local noise regimes.

item.title: esQueranto: Differentiable Structured Quantum Light for Automated Scientific Discovery
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Unified differentiable simulation combines Fock-state quantum optics with structured-light propagation in JAX, allowing mode-dependent Gouy phases and lenses to directly alter Fock bases and quantum interference.

Grade 0.425 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Marcello Armezzani, Tareq Jaouni, Pontus Lindgren, Sören Arlt, Mario Krenn, Xuemei Gu

Figure

Heralded radial-mode sorting output probabilities versus dephasing strength γ=1−ξ. Single-photon input routing degrades to equal split (1/2), while two-photon inputs (p=0,p=1) approach 3/4 anti-bunching due to common-path phase noise.

Asks

How can photon-number quantum optics, open-system noise, and transverse spatial-mode propagation be unified into a single differentiable simulator for automated experimental design?

Before

Existing tools separately model photonic quantum optics (MrMustard, Perceval) or wave optics (XLuminA, Chromatix) without combining Fock states and spatial propagation in a differentiable framework.

But

Classical pump approximation for squeezing; paraxial and Laguerre-Gauss beam assumptions without full non-paraxial vectorial propagation or open-system matter couplings.

Tools

JAX automatic differentiation · Fock basis expansion · Laguerre-Gauss spatial mode propagation · interferometric radial-mode sorters

Code. https://github.com/artificial-scientist-lab/esQueranto

Abstract

Uncovering new phenomena in nature requires experiments. For centuries, their design has been exclusively a human endeavor. Today, a new paradigm is emerging in which artificial intelligence and computational methods can design experiments themselves. Realizing this form of automated scientific discovery requires simulators that are sufficiently expressive to represent the diverse physical processes and couplings from which new experiments can be constructed. In this direction, we introduce textscesQueranto, a differentiable software that brings photon-number quantum optics and structured-light propagation into a common description, allowing the spatial evolution of light to directly influence non-classical quantum states and their interference. textscesQueranto is implemented in JAX, providing automatic differentiation and hardware-accelerated evaluation for optimization and automated search. We demonstrate the framework across a broad range of quantum-optical applications that exercise complementary aspects of its physical description. By combining quantum and structured-light physics within a single differentiable simulator, textscesQueranto takes an important step towards the dream of a foundational simulator in physics.

item.title: First-quantized quantum simulation with non-local potentials by matrix-product-state encoding
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Matrix product state encoding of non-local pseudopotentials yields a single Trotter step circuit depth of O(deg⁡(Vloc)ndeg⁡(Vloc)+8Lnnatomχ2+2n2). For n=7 qubits, depth is 1,747 versus 23,775 for direct unitary decomposition.

Grade 0.424 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Kazuki Tsuoka, Taichi Kosugi, Masari Watanabe, Hirofumi Nishi, Yu-ichiro Matsushita

Figure

Circuit depth of a single Trotter step plotted against qubit count n for MPS bond dimensions χ=2,4,6,8 compared to standard unitary decomposition.

Asks

How to efficiently implement arbitrary non-local pseudopotentials within first-quantized quantum chemistry dynamics circuits?

Before

Direct dense unitary decomposition scaled exponentially as O(4n), reaching circuit depth 23,775 at n=7.

But

Demonstrated for a one-dimensional single-electron hydrogen ionization model in momentum representation. Assumes polynomial local potential Vloc and low bond dimension saturation for smooth projectors.

Tools

matrix product state encoding · first-order Trotterization · binary-encoded wave functions · Qiskit transpiler unitary synthesis

Abstract

Quantum simulations based on first-quantized approaches can offer lower space and gate complexities than second-quantized approaches. The gate requirements for these simulations can be further reduced by employing pseudopotentials, a technique widely used in classical quantum chemistry calculations to decrease the number of simulated electrons. However, implementing pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging due to their non-local nature. In this study, we proposed a method to efficiently implement non-local potentials using matrix product state (MPS) encoding. MPS encoding allows us to efficiently implement a Trotter step operator with a circuit depth of O(deg(V_loc) n^(deg(V_loc)) + 8Lnn_atomχ² + 2n²), where deg(V_loc) is the degree of the polynomial local potential, n_atom is the number of atoms in the system, L is the maximum number of projector functions across all atoms, and n is the number of qubits used to represent the binary-encoded wave function in one-dimensional space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of the ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse. Our results showed that MPS encoding significantly reduces the required circuit depth compared to a direct unitary decomposition, providing a pathway for practical first-quantized simulations.

item.title: Quantum Circuit Pruning: From NISQ Architectures to Fault-Tolerant Operations
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Compares omission fidelity bound cos2⁡(θ/2) against hardware routing costs, cutting two-qubit gate count by up to 48.6% and increasing circuit fidelity by up to 47.7% on NISQ benchmarks.

Grade 0.409 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits” · Pau Escofet, Carmen G. Almudéver, Sergi Abadal, Eduard Alarcón

Figure

Two-qubit CX gate counts (top) and final circuit state fidelities (bottom) plotted across 4- to 14-qubit benchmark algorithms for unpruned compilation versus the proposed routing-aware pruning.

Asks

Can quantum circuit gate pruning be dynamically guided by routing distance and execution noise in both NISQ and fault-tolerant regimes?

Before

was offline gate pruning considering only rotation angle θ without target hardware connectivity constraints

But

Evaluated via simulations on 4–14 qubit NISQ circuits and proxy two-CNOT lattice surgery paths rather than full end-to-end FTQC compilation; assumes fixed 1.25× SWAP routing overhead multiplier for NISQ heuristics.

Tools

Route-Forcing algorithm · Stim and PyMatching simulation · TQEC lattice surgery · Qiskit density-matrix simulation

Abstract

We present a routing-aware pruning strategy for quantum circuits that selectively removes parametric two-qubit gates whose computational contribution is outweighed by the fidelity cost of their execution, and assess it across both Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) and fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) architectures. Each two-qubit gate of a circuit is evaluated by comparing an architecture-independent lower bound on the fidelity cost of omitting the gate against a hardware-specific model for the routing execution cost in each setting. We additionally provide an analytical characterization of the pruning boundary as a function of rotation angle, qubit distance, and hardware noise. Simulations on benchmark circuits demonstrate gate count reductions of up to 48.6% and fidelity improvements of up to 47.7% in the NISQ regime, while a feasibility analysis on FT hardware indicates that pruning is expected to remain relevant across a range of code distances and physical error rates. These results establish routing-aware pruning as a practical and unified compilation strategy across the quantum computing stack.

item.title: Nonlinear collective-spin dynamics for quantum-enhanced sensing in solid-state platforms
item.description:
Worth a look review — Connects nonlinear collective-spin twisting dynamics to solid-state platforms, surveying spin squeezing and quantum enhancements across NV ensembles (demonstrating −0.50±0.13 dB squeezing or 6.7(6)% amplification), donor spins in 28Si, and magnetic Kittel modes.

Grade 0.408 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Le Bin Ho

Figure

Wineland squeezing parameter ξ2 plotted against scaled evolution time χt, comparing noise reduction capabilities of one-axis twisting, two-axis twisting, and two-axis non-twisting dynamics.

Asks

How do microscopic interactions, disorder, and decoherence dictate the generation of quantum-enhanced metrological states via nonlinear collective-spin dynamics in solid-state platforms?

But

Spatial disorder and inhomogeneous couplings break collective permutation symmetry; technical noise, control errors, and decoherence cap effective nonlinear interaction time.

Tools

Dicke basis collective spin formalism · one-axis and two-axis twisting (OAT/TAT) · Floquet pulse engineering · nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center ensembles · tqix simulation package

Abstract

Collective spin systems in solid-state materials are promising platforms for quantum-enhanced sensing. In systems such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, donor spins in silicon, and magnetic materials, interactions among many spins can generate collective quantum correlations that improve measurement precision beyond the standard quantum limit. This tutorial develops an intuitive, materials-oriented framework for understanding these effects through nonlinear collective-spin dynamics. We show how nonlinear interactions reshape collective spin states in phase space, redistribute quantum fluctuations, and generate metrologically useful states such as spin-squeezed and entangled states. We then connect these ideal collective dynamics to microscopic interactions and realistic solid-state systems, discussing how interaction strength, disorder, decoherence, and experimental control affect sensing performance. Different platforms and experiments are compared to highlight key material properties, advantages, and limitations. The tutorial focuses on a materials-oriented understanding of nonlinear collective-spin sensing, rather than a comprehensive comparison of experimental platforms or a practical guide to sensing experiments.

item.title: Experimental quantification of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Direct measurement of basis-independent mean robustness of set coherence yields ℛ1(ϱ1→)=0.5 for a two-state set and ℛ1(ϱ2→)=10227≈0.524 for a three-state set via interference visibility.

Grade 0.403 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Long-distance quantum communication with atomic ensembles and linear optics” · Tianle Zheng, Liangsheng Li, Wenting Zhou, Chengjie Zhang

Figure

Average interference visibility V2=(V3+V4+V5)/3 as a function of half-wave plate rotation angle α3 for the 3-state set. Experimental data match the theoretical minimum ℛ1(ϱ2→)≈0.524.

Asks

Can basis-independent quantum coherence for an ensemble of quantum states be quantified directly in experiment?

But

Pure qubit states restricted to the X-Z plane of the Bloch sphere.

Tools

Sagnac interferometer · spontaneous parametric down-conversion · PPKTP crystal · single-photon detectors

Abstract

We present a direct experimental verification of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states in a basis-independent manner. We find that the theory of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states matches our experimental results perfectly and can be applied to protocols like BB84 and quantum secure direct communication. Using a Sagnac interferometer, we experimentally quantify the quantum coherence for two sets of experimental states. Moreover, we introduce a novel application of set coherence, illustrating that the states employed in the BB84 protocol exhibit maximal set coherence. Our results pave the way for wider applications of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states, including quantum key distribution protocols and probabilistic quantum cloning.

item.title: Less precise but less noisy: local circuits for momentum-space state preparation and measurement
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Adiabatic state preparation reaches lower energies than Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT) on noisy hardware for tight-binding chains with N⪆20 qubits at equal two-qubit gate counts. Noise heating per two-qubit gate scales as 𝒪(1) for FFT but remains constant 𝒪(1/N) for adiabatic evolution.

Grade 0.400 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Etienne Granet, Henrik Dreyer

Figure

Measured energy density and energy increase per two-qubit gate versus system size N for FFT and adiabatic evolution on Quantinuum H2-2. Shows adiabatic evolution achieving lower energies than FFT above N≈20 due to constant heating per gate compared to linear growth for FFT.

Asks

How does circuit noise sensitivity compare between high-precision Fermionic Fourier Transforms and local Hamiltonian simulation or adiabatic evolution for state preparation and measurement?

Before

FFT state preparation and momentum measurement (Ref [31]) exhibited high noise sensitivity due to global error propagation.

But

Antiperiodic boundary conditions, tight-binding free-fermion chains, non-post-selected initial state |+...+⟩ introducing tiny energy shifts scaling as 1/N, fixed number of measurement shots (300 to 375).

Tools

Quantinuum System Model H2-2 trapped-ion processor · Adiabatic evolution Trotter circuits · Momentum Distribution from Local Measurements (MDLM) · Jordan-Wigner transformation

Abstract

Quantum algorithms are usually optimized for gate count or circuit depth. We find on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer that for a tight-binding chain ground state preparation, there is a system size N beyond which the adiabatic evolution reaches significantly lower energies than the Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT), with the same number of gates, and with the same circuit depth. We attribute this high noise sensitivity of the FFT to its high precision, being able to distinguish momenta by 1/N. This high resolution in momentum space requires long-range couplings in real space, which propagates errors faster. In contrast, although local and physical circuits such as the adiabatic evolution have a coarser momentum resolution, they also propagate errors more slowly. For physical applications, high momentum resolution is rarely required and is often worth trading for low noise sensitivity. We also introduce a momentum measurement scheme that although less precise than FFT, is less costly and less noisy. We show that it achieves better performance than FFT for spectral function measurement on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer. Our work emphasizes the importance of reducing the noise sensitivity of quantum algorithms, beyond the number of gates or circuit depth.
